text: Reverse a string given as a character array, s. Do it in place, with constant extra memory.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. In place with constant extra memory rules out building a reversed copy — I should mutate s directly, with just a couple of index variables. And it's a char array, any printable ASCII, right?
Then this is the classic opposite-direction two pointers: one from each end, swap and converge.

Let me name the alternatives. A reversed copy is linear space — it fails the constraint. Recursion that swaps the ends is in place for the data, but it uses a linear-depth call stack. This problem reminds me of the opposite-direction two-pointer pattern, because reversing just means the first and last characters trade places, then the next pair in, and so on. So: l at the start, r at the end, swap and move inward until they meet. Linear time, constant space, no stack.

Here's the plan. One: set l to zero and r to n minus one. Two: while l is less than r, swap s of l and s of r. Three: move l right and r left. One thing worth flagging — the condition is l less than r, which handles both parities: an even length ends with the pointers crossing, and an odd length stops at l equals r, since the middle character is its own pair and needs no swap. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me write the explicit two-pointer version. Two indices start at the ends; each pass swaps them and steps both inward, until they meet. One detail worth flagging — standard reverse on begin and end would do exactly this in one line. I wrote it out to show the mechanism, because variants that reverse only some of the characters build on this same loop.

Let's dry-run hello, expecting o, l, l, e, h. Two swaps — h with o, then e with l — and the row that matters is the last one: both pointers land on index two, l less than r is false, so the loop stops. The middle l stays put, and we get olleh. That matches. Corner cases: an even length like a, b, c, d becomes d, c, b, a, with the pointers crossing. A single character, or an empty array, never enters the loop.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — n over two swaps, with each pointer walking half the array. Space is constant — two index variables, in place, no stack. Oh, one more thing — this converging-pointers skeleton is the backbone of the whole two-pointer family: swap the ends to reverse, compare the ends to check a palindrome, or add the ends to search a sorted array for a target sum. Same loop, different middle step.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: ruling out the copy and the recursion on the constant-space constraint, the single l less than r condition covering both parities, and connecting the skeleton to the broader two-pointer family. Good work.
